Mallam Town is a real place in the Greater Accra Region. Every person, family and event in this book is invented, and no resemblance to any person living or dead is intended.

For the ones who were in the room
and were never asked.

Note on this edition

Mallam Town is a story for readers of about twelve to fifteen — the Junior High School years, and the upper end of primary. It is set in a real township on the road out of Accra, and nearly all of it happens within walking distance of one compound house.

The reading level. The book is fifteen chapters and about 15,600 words, with one illustration opening each chapter. Sentences average between nine and fifteen words. The measured reading level sits at Flesch–Kincaid 4.3, which means a pupil in JHS 1 should be able to read it independently and a weaker reader in JHS 3 comfortably. Nothing in the book requires a dictionary, but there is a glossary at the back for the Ghanaian words, the harder English, and the names.

What the book is careful about. This is a story about a man who is wrongly accused and a woman who disappears, and both of those could have been written brutally. They have not been. There is no sexual content in this book. There is no description of the injuries people receive, beyond what is needed to understand what happened. There is no mob, and nobody in this story is hurt by a crowd. When the worst thing in the book happens, it is described by its sound and by the faces of the people watching it, and not by anything the reader is made to look at.

1

A note on Nene. Nene is a traditional herbalist — a healer who treats people with plants, and who has been doing it for forty years. This book uses the words herbs, medicine, and her knowledge. It does not use fetish, juju, witch, charms, magic, or spirits, about her or about anyone else. This is a deliberate choice, and it is worth explaining to a class: those words are used carelessly about traditional healers, and none of them are needed to tell this story. Nene is not mysterious. She is old, her knees hurt, she is paid in yam, and she is the most competent person in the book.

The two questions the book asks. The first is: what is the difference between keeping the peace and keeping quiet? Kwame spends twenty years being called the Peacemaker before he finds out that they are not the same thing. The second is: whose knowledge counts? The police have a ledger. Nene has forty years of listening. The book’s answer is that you need both, and that a town which only believes one of them will lose people.

How to use this book in class. There are discussion questions at the back, arranged in four parts of three or four chapters each, mixing comprehension with questions that have more than one good answer. There are seven writing tasks — including the radio correction that Chief Inspector Nanfuri has to read out, and the letter that Maame Adjoa takes to the police station. There is a map on the endpapers; pupils can mark on it where each chapter happens. And there is a glossary, which includes a table of the Akan day-names — every major character in this book is named for the day of the week they were born, and working out which day is a good first lesson.

2

A note on the English. The dialogue in this book is written in the English that Ghanaians actually speak, and the narration is written in standard Ghanaian English. Neither is a mistake, and neither is a deficiency. Both are on the page on purpose.

3

The people in this book

Kwame Asante. forty-four, a taxi driver. Twenty years at the rank in Mallam Town. Everyone calls him the Peacemaker, because he is the man people bring their small quarrels to.

Mansa Asante. his wife. Thirty-eight, and deliberate in everything she does.

Nene. seventy-one. A traditional herbalist. She has bad knees, a stick, a basket, and a mortar worn smooth on one side.

Chief Inspector Nanfuri. head of the Mallam Town Police Post. In his forties, and tired in the way of a man with too many open files.

Inspector Adzo Mensah. about thirty. She has read every page of a file nobody asked her to read.

Kwabena Dapaah. fifty-four. A carpenter, built like the thing he works with. He comes to Nene about his hands.

Yaw Sarpong. fifty-six. A landlord. He owns the houses behind the cemetery — the ones that have been going up for four years and have never got past the first floor.

Papa Kofi and Mr. Tee. drivers at the rank.

Maame Adjoa and Maame Akua. two mothers. Their sons stopped coming home.

Efua Nanfuri. twenty-four. She does not appear in this book, and the whole of it happens because of her.

The Old Woman on the veranda. she has not walked past her own gate in two years.

4

A note on the names

Most of the people in this book have Akan names, and an Akan name often tells you the day of the week a person was born.

Born onA boy is calledA girl is called
SundayKwesi, KwasiAkosua
MondayKojo, KwadwoAdwoa, Adjoa, Adzo
TuesdayKwabenaAbena
WednesdayKwaku, KwekuAkua
ThursdayYaw, EkowYaa
FridayKofiAfua, Efua
SaturdayKwameAma

So Kwame was born on a Saturday, Kwabena on a Tuesday, and Kofi on a Friday. Adjoa and Adzo are the same name in two different languages. Ekow and Yaw were both born on a Thursday.

Nene is not a day-name. It is a Ga-Dangme word, and it is a title of respect — for a chief, for a queenmother, or for any elder. In this book it is not really her name. It is what you call an old woman you are about to ask a favour of.

Mansa means “of three” — the name given to a third-born girl.

5
Chapter One

The Peacemaker

Mallam Town woke up at four and did not wait for anybody.

By seven the taxi rank was already full of dust and shouting and horns. Old yellow taxis nosed in one after another, their paint faded by the sun. Drivers leaned against bonnets arguing about fuel prices. A kenkey seller went past calling out her prices. At the corner a preacher's public address system coughed into life, far too early, and a hundred people pretended not to hear it.

Kwame Asante sat on an overturned plastic crate beside his own taxi, polishing his side mirror with a rag. The rag was far cleaner than the car deserved.

1

When the preacher got going, Kwame listened for a while, and then opened the bible on his knee to check the verse. He did this most mornings. Not to argue — to see whether the man was telling the truth. If he found that he was not, Kwame simply stopped listening. He had never once said anything to anybody about it.

He was forty-four, tall and lanky, with quiet hands and a face that did not hurry to show what he was thinking. Twenty years at this rank had taught him that most arguments are not about what they say they are about, and that nearly all of them go quiet on their own if nobody feeds them.

Peace, in Kwame's life, meant keeping quiet long enough for other people's noise to die down.

He did not yet know how much that belief was going to cost him.

At the other end of the rank, Papa Kofi and Mr. Tee were arguing again.

"You are telling me the man paid you for three?" Mr. Tee said.

"He paid me for two and walked away on the third," Papa Kofi said. "So who is the thief here?"

They had been at it since six. The argument had started somewhere else entirely and had only now found its way to the station.

Kwame did not look up from his mirror.

"It was not my customer," Mr. Tee said.

"It was yours."

"It was not."

Kwame waited until they had both run out of words. Then he said, without raising his voice:

2

"Was the man wearing a blue shirt?"

Mr. Tee turned. "Yes —"

"Then that is the one Papa Kofi dropped at the junction an hour ago. Not yours."

A beat.

Mr. Tee opened his mouth. Closed it again. He muttered something about the price of fuel and walked off to his car.

Papa Kofi grinned and clapped Kwame on the shoulder.

"Peacemaker," he said. "Every time."

Kwame shrugged and went back to the mirror.

It was true, what they called him. At the rank, in the compound where he lived, even at the roadside food stalls — Kwame was the man people brought their small quarrels to. He listened. He did not shout. He settled things. He had been doing it so long that he hardly noticed anymore.

That evening, at the compound house off the main road, his wife Mansa sat on their small porch braiding her hair.

Mansa Asante was thirty-eight and deliberate in every motion. Even braiding her hair she did it slowly, carefully, as if the world would wait for her to finish. A small mirror was propped against the wall. A pot simmered on a single gas stove beside her. The smell of stew mixed with something else — her perfume, sweet and strong, filling the small room before you saw her face properly.

She had changed her cloth while he was washing. He noticed it and did not think about it.

"My credit finished this morning," she said, not looking up. "Yours?"

3

He slid it across the table without a word. She used it for a moment, then set it down.

Then: "The balance."

He heard it and did not answer.

"Kwame. The MoMo balance."

It was the second time this month she had asked in that particular voice — the one that was not really a question.

"Ei," he said, and went on washing.

She said nothing more. She went back to her hair. The pot went on simmering. The two of them sat in the same small room not saying the thing they were both thinking, which was what they had been doing for months.

Later, the wall clock read 11:42 p.m.

He could not have said afterwards which of them had said the thing that finished it. It was the same argument they had been having for months, arriving at the same place it always arrived. And when it was over Kwame stood up and walked out — not to punish her, not to end anything, but because he did not want to fuel it. Twenty years at the rank had taught him that the fastest way to end a quarrel is to stop being in the room with it.

Outside, in the compound yard, the Old Woman on the veranda watched him pass. She was somewhere in her seventies, thin as a broomstick, and she sat in that same chair every evening, watching everything and saying almost nothing. Her chair creaked once as Kwame went by. She did not speak.

Kwame reached the rusted compound gate.

4

Every night when he came home late, this gate screamed — a long metal shriek that woke half the compound. So Kwame had learned to push it slowly, gently, muffling the sound with his own hand. The way he had learned to do everything in his life: quietly, and at his own expense.

Tonight it did not scream.

He pushed it the way he always did and it opened in silence. For half a second some part of him noticed. Then he was thinking about the argument again, and the half-second passed, and he walked out into the road.

Fifty metres down, he stopped.

"My phone," he said to the empty road.

And he turned back.

[984 words — budget 800]

5
Chapter Two

The Empty Room

He walked back the way he had come, and by the time he reached the compound the anger had already drained out of his shoulders, the way it always did once he put distance between himself and a fight.

That was why he walked out. Not to punish Mansa. To cool his own head.

The yard was dark. The Old Woman's chair was empty. Somewhere a radio played too low to hear the words.

He pushed open the door to their room.

Darkness.

Wrong darkness. He had left the light on. He knew he had left the light on, the way you know a thing you did with your own hand thirty seconds ago.

"Mansa?"

Nothing.

He found the bedside table by memory.

6

His phone was there where he had left it.

It was warm.

He stood in the dark with it in his hand, feeling the warmth of it the way you feel the side of a cup, and not understanding for a moment what warmth meant. Somebody had been holding it. Somebody had set it down recently enough that it had not had time to cool.

He thumbed the screen alive and swept its weak light across the room.

Empty bed. Empty corner. The plastic chair, empty.

He found the wall switch.

Light flooded the room.

Still empty.

Her perfume was everywhere. That was the thing he could not make sense of — the perfume, recent and close and thick in the air, as if she had only just been standing exactly where he was standing, as if she had stepped sideways into the wall. He could smell her and not find her. And there was only one door.

He dialled.

It rang once.

REJECTED.

He looked at the screen the way a man looks at a thing that has just done something impossible.

He tried again.

REJECTED.

The screen stayed lit in his hand. Under his own two calls, the log showed a number he did not recognise, called that night.

He looked at the number.

He did not look at it properly. He was frightened, and a frightened man does not read small print — he looks for the next thing to do.

He went back out into the yard.

"Mansa!"

7

Nothing. Not a window opened. Not a voice. He crossed to the Old Woman's door and knocked, and heard the chair creak inside, and then nothing at all.

"Auntie. Have you seen Mansa?"

A long pause. Then her voice, thin through the wood, irritable with sleep.

"I have heard nothing tonight. Not even the gate."

He stood in the dark yard with that.

Not even the gate.

He put the phone in his pocket and went out to the taxi.

The engine caught on the second try, coughing, then settling.

He drove slowly at first, along the main road with the windows down, saying her name at the empty roadside the way a man says a name into a room he already knows is empty. Then faster, out towards the unlit stretches where he thought she might have walked.

He would drive every street in Mallam Town if he had to.

He did not know that by going to look for his wife, he was driving into the thing that would take everything else.

[550 words — budget 700]

8
Chapter Three

Dangerous Lane

Dangerous Lane was not a lane, exactly. It was the stretch of road between the last compound and the cemetery wall, where the streetlights gave up and the bush came close on both sides.

Everyone in Mallam Town knew not to stop there after dark.

Kwame drove it anyway, leaning forward over the wheel, scanning both sides for a flash of her cloth, her shape walking, anything. He had driven it a hundred times at that hour and had never once thought about it — which is what twenty years does to a man. It makes the dangerous ordinary.

He was thinking her name so hard that he almost did not see the headlights.

They came up behind him too close and too fast.

9

He checked the mirror. Moved over. They came with him.

Before he could decide what that meant, a second vehicle cut in ahead of him and swung across the lane, and there was nowhere left to go.

Kwame stopped.

His hands stayed on the wheel.

Two men and a woman got out of the car in front. Unhurried. That was the thing he would remember afterwards — how unhurried they were, the way people are when they have done this before and know exactly how long it takes.

One of the men carried a tyre iron. The woman held a pistol low against her thigh, almost casual, like a handbag.

Kwame rolled down his window. Years of difficult passengers had taught him a certain calm.

"I don't have any —"

"Step out," the Woman said.

He did.

There was no argument left in him, and it was not because he had given up. It was because he had done this calculation a hundred times — with angry passengers, with drunk men at the rank, with his own wife shouting at him at twenty to midnight — and the mathematics had never once favoured pride.

Somebody took his phone out of his pocket without asking.

"Face the car."

He faced the car.

What followed was fast, and almost businesslike. Professional. A blow to the ribs — controlled, not wild. Another. Somebody grabbed the back of his shirt and it tore. A third man pinned his arms behind him before either hand was touched.

"Not the face," the Man with the Tyre Iron said.

10

"Leave his hands," the Woman said.

He did not understand why, then. He would understand later.

His shoulder went. He heard it go — a sound like a door being shut in another room — and then the ground came up and hit him, and something sharp took the skin above his left eye, and the rest of it happened somewhere below the level of thought.

Afterwards there was the sound of his own engine starting.

His own car. The car Mansa had bought him to make them money, pulling away into the dark with somebody else at the wheel.

He did not get up. He could not. For a long time he lay in the dust beside the road, listening to his own breathing, and to the insects, and to Mallam Town continuing somewhere beyond the lane, uncaring.

Then silence.

Not quiet. Mallam Town was never quiet. But the particular silence of a place where something has finished happening and the dust has not settled yet.

A few feet from his hand, face-down in the dust where somebody had dropped it in the hurry of leaving, a phone began to ring.

It rang twice, and stopped.

Nobody was there to hear it.

[583 words — budget 750]

11
Chapter Four

Nene

She was out before the sun, because the bark she wanted came off the tree behind the cemetery, and it came off easier before the day got hot and the sap rose.

Nene was not her name, not really. Nene was what you called an old woman you were about to ask a favour of.

Her knees had their own opinion about the cemetery path. She told them what she thought of it and went on anyway. The basket was light going out, which was the only thing going out had to recommend it.

The road was the colour of nothing yet. Light enough to see the potholes. Not light enough to see into them.

There was a shape in the gutter on Dangerous Lane.

12

She had walked past shapes before. Mallam Town put things in its gutters and expected you to step over them. But this one lay at an angle no drunk man lies at, with one arm underneath him where an arm had no business being.

She set the basket down. It took her a while to kneel, and it hurt, and she said so to nobody.

A few feet away, face-down in the dust where somebody had dropped it in the hurry of leaving, lay a phone.

Nene looked at it for a moment. Then she picked it up and put it in the pocket of her cloth. A phone is a useful thing to have. And a man whose phone is gone is a man nobody can call, which suits somebody.

She turned him over by the good arm.

"Ei," she said. "Who did this to you?"

He did not answer. One eye was shut, his breathing was shallow, and there was dust in his mouth.

Then the light moved, just enough, and she saw his face.

This was Kwame. The taxi driver. The Peacemaker. The one they all said never raised his voice — who sat at the rank with a rag and a mirror and settled other people's quarrels the way other men shell groundnuts.

"So," Nene said to the empty road. "Even you."

She could not lift him. She was seventy-one and he was a grown man, and the arithmetic was not complicated.

What she could do was shout.

13

Two boys going to fetch water heard her and came running. Then a woman from the compound. Then — because this is how things happen in Mallam Town, quickly and without anybody arranging it — a man with a cart. They got him to her compound between them, the way you move a sack of cement, except more carefully.

Her room smelled of bark. Herbs hung in bundles from a line across the ceiling. There was a mortar in the corner, worn smooth on one side, and a shelf of small bottles, each with a name scratched into the glass.

She sent everyone out except the boy who looked least likely to faint.

The shoulder came first. A shoulder out of its socket will not wait, and it will not wait for anybody. She had set her nephew's the year he fell out of the mango tree, and two of the market women's, and one belonging to a man who never thanked her and never would.

"Hold him," she said.

She put her hands where they belonged and told him it would hurt, though he could not hear her, and pulled.

It went back with a sound that made her own bones ache in sympathy.

The boy made a noise and sat down hard on the floor.

"If you are going to be sick," Nene said, "be sick outside."

14

The ribs came next, and there was less she could do for ribs. Bruised, she thought, not broken — a broken rib has a sound to it when a man breathes, and his breathing was shallow but clean. She bound him with a length of cloth, not too tight.

The cut above the eye she cleaned with water she had boiled that morning and left to cool.

Afterwards she sat back on her heels and turned his hands over, palm up, the way you check a fish.

Not marked. Whoever had done this had left his hands alone. She did not know why, and then she did: a taxi driver needs his hands. Needs his face too, if he wants to work again.

These people were not animals. They were workers, doing a job.

Then she put two fingers against the side of his neck and held them there, counting to herself the way her mother had taught her to count a thing that was still running.

Slow. But there.

Then she held his head in both hands, carefully, and turned it, and looked into his eyes.

One pupil was sluggish. The other was not.

"If his head were bleeding inside," she said to the boy, "no leaf would help him. That one is for the hospital, and I will not pretend otherwise. Go and watch the road. If a car comes, tell me."

That is the whole of it, really. Knowing which things are yours.

15

Then the bark, pounded in the mortar worn smooth on one side, made into a paste, laid on the bruises and held with a clean cloth. It was not a cure. It was the difference between a body that swells and a body that does not, and anybody who tells you otherwise is selling something.

She checked his eyes every hour through the night. By dawn both pupils were the same size, and she let out a breath she had been holding since the gutter.

"You were lucky," she said to him, though he still could not hear her. "I was ready to send you."

Pain arrived before memory did.

A deep, sick throb in the ribs. A hot tightness around the left eye. And his right shoulder — his right shoulder was simply not there, and then it was, and then it hurt in a way he could not have described to anybody.

He tried to sit up. The room tilted. He fell back and said a word he had not said in twenty years.

"Lie still," somebody said. "You will open the cut."

The ceiling was not his ceiling. The light was wrong. Bundles of something hung from a line above him, and the room smelled of bark and of something else, green and crushed.

There was a small plastic chair. An old woman sat in it, asleep, or pretending.

He lay back and closed his eye that worked, and said, without meaning to:

"Mansa."

16

It was evening when he woke properly. Light the colour of dust coming through the window. The old woman was awake, grinding something in the corner, and did not turn around.

He lay still for a while and took stock.

He was alive. That seemed worth something, and he gave thanks for it quietly, the way he always had, to himself, without moving his lips.

The grinding stopped.

"The one who made the tree," she said, "and the one who made the leaf. You think they are different people?"

He did not know what to say to that.

She turned around then, and he saw her properly for the first time. Small. Seventy-odd. Hands that looked like they had spent a life doing things. A stick against the wall beside her that she plainly resented.

"I am Nene," she said. "You are in my compound. You were in the gutter on Dangerous Lane with no taxi and half your shirt gone, and I did not think it was a good night to leave you there."

"Why not the hospital?" Kwame said.

She shrugged.

"And then the police come," she said, "and they ask questions, and you are a man with bruises and no answers. I have watched that happen. I am not watching it again."

She went back to grinding.

Kwame lay still. His ribs ached when he breathed too deep. Outside, Mallam Town was going about its evening — a radio, a pot lid, somebody laughing too loud. Ordinary life, continuing, as if nothing had happened.

17

"I have to report it anyway," he said.

"I know," Nene said. "I will take you on Thursday. Today you cannot walk to that road and back."

He closed his eye that worked.

"Thursday," he said.

"Thursday," she said.

[1,390 words — budget 1,000]

18
Chapter Five

The Report

Nene walked with him as far as the main road and stopped there.

"I am not going any further," she said. "I have been in that building once in my life, and once was plenty."

"Will you wait?"

"I will wait."

She sat down on the low wall by the drainage ditch, the way old women sit, as though the wall had been put there for her, and took a piece of bark from her pocket and began to work at it with her thumbnail.

Kwame went on alone.

19

The Mallam Town Police Post was a squat concrete building with paint peeling at the corners. A ceiling fan went round and round above the counter too slowly to matter, pushing hot air from one side of the room to the other.

Kwame leaned on the counter and moved stiffly, because every breath caught somewhere on the left side of his ribs.

The Desk Officer did not look up more than was necessary. He had a thick ledger open in front of him and a blue Biro that skipped.

"Make and year?"

"Toyota. Old one," Kwame said. "Dent on the rear passenger door. You'll know it before you ask the plate number."

The officer wrote. Kwame watched the Biro skip and thought: write it properly. Write it properly. This is the only thing anybody is ever going to write down.

"Colour?"

"Yellow. Faded."

"Where taken?"

"Dangerous Lane. About half past twelve Monday night. Three of them. Two men and a woman. They had a pistol."

The officer's head came up at that, and went down again.

"And the wife?"

Kwame opened his mouth.

20

How do you say it? How do you say to a man writing in a ledger: I went out to cool my head after an argument. I came back ten minutes later. She was gone and her perfume was still in the air. I called her twice and she rejected the call both times. Then I went out to look for her and they took the car and left me in the gutter, and now I do not know where either of them is.

You cannot fit that into the lines of a police form.

"She's missing," Kwame said finally. "Since Monday night."

The officer nodded and wrote. He said it the way men say things they do not expect to revisit.

"We'll log it."

Behind the counter, through a half-open office door, Kwame caught a glimpse of the senior officer.

Chief Inspector Nanfuri was in his forties and tired in the unremarkable way of a man with too many open files. He stood at his desk with the telephone at his ear and his back half turned, and he said into it, in a voice that was not unkind:

"I know. I know I said I would. Just — give me till Friday."

Then he glanced up. His eye went past Kwame to the counter and the ledger, and found nothing there that needed him, and he turned back to the wall.

Kwame had the strangest feeling, standing there — that the man in that room was carrying something. He could not have said what. It was in the set of the shoulders.

21

Then the moment passed, and the feeling went with it, and Kwame forgot about it entirely until much later, when there was no forgetting left to do.

The officer tore a slip off the pad and handed it over.

A case number.

It felt thin in his hand. Too thin to hold everything that had happened.

Nene was still on the wall when he came out. She did not ask how it had gone. She looked at his face, put the bark back in her pocket, and stood up, and they walked back to her compound together in the heat.

Five days passed.

Five days in which Kwame went to the rank and asked, and the drivers shook their heads, and Papa Kofi said the thing everybody says — "Chaley, maybe she went to her sister's, women do that" — and Kwame said she would have answered her phone, and Papa Kofi had no answer for that.

Five days in which Nene asked after Mansa the way old women do, which is to say between other words, while measuring bark or grinding something in the corner, so that nobody listening would have known she was asking anything at all.

Five days in which nobody from the Mallam Town Police Post came to the compound. Nobody walked the lane. Nobody knocked on a door.

On the fifth evening Kwame went back to the room.

He stood in the doorway for a long time with the light on.

22

The perfume was fading. It had been so strong that first night you could almost taste it, and now it was only there if you went looking for it, and soon it would not be there at all.

Nene was right, he thought.

What he did not think, because it did not occur to him, was that Nene was usually right.

[841 words — budget 750]

23
Chapter Six

A Face on the Radio

The radio was always on.

It sat on the shelf in Nene's room between a tin of something and a bottle with a name scratched into the glass, and it played from the moment she got up until the batteries gave out, which they did most afternoons. Nene said she did not listen to it. She had it on the way other people have a door open.

That morning Kwame was trying to help.

He had got as far as lifting the pestle over the mortar with his right hand and bringing it down once, badly, before the shoulder said no.

"Sit," Nene said, without turning round.

"I have been sitting for a week."

24

"Then sit for two. The body is not a thing you hurry. I have watched men make themselves worse being in a hurry to be better."

He sat.

It was just after seven. The station played highlife for a while, and then the newsreader's voice came on, and Nene reached over and turned it up a little, the way people do when they are not really listening.

"—the body of a young woman was discovered early this morning in a vehicle abandoned near the Mallam Town cemetery road. Mansa

The room had one window and the window had no glass, and the light coming through it made a bright square on the wall.

Mansa watched the square.

In the morning it was on the floor. By the middle of the day it had climbed the wall. By evening it was gone. That was how she knew what day it was. That was the whole of what she had.

33

There was a bucket in the corner. There was a mat. The door opened outwards and locked on the outside, and it was opened three times a day by a man with a bowl, who did not speak, who set the bowl down just inside the door and took the previous one away, and who had never once looked at her face.

She had stopped asking him questions on the second day. Not because she was brave. Because the not-speaking was worse than anything he could have said to her.

On the eighth day she heard a radio.

It came from somewhere beyond the wall — a windowsill, a trotro going past, she could not tell which. She pressed her ear against the plaster the way she had pressed it as a girl when her mother had visitors, and she heard the tail of a news bulletin, and then, at eight o'clock, the thing itself.

"The Ghana Police Service is seeking Kwame Asante, a taxi driver of Mallam Town, in connection with the robbery and the death of Efua Nanfuri, twenty-four —"

She stood very still.

34

It was stupid. It was not possible. Kwame Asante could not rob anybody. Kwame Asante, who had once spent a whole afternoon teaching a boy at the rank to tie a proper knot because the boy's knot kept slipping. Kwame, who would not raise his voice to a drunk man. Kwame, who had sat across from her for months and said nothing while she said everything, and who had walked out of their room at twenty to twelve on a Monday night with his shoulders up around his ears and had not —

Had not come back.

That was the thing she could not get past.

He had not come back. She had stood at the gate and watched the road for ten minutes, or twenty, or an hour — she had lost the shape of it — and he had not come back. And then a car had stopped at the end of the lane, and a man she knew had got out of it, and she had opened her mouth to greet him, and he had taken her arm.

And now Kwame was on the radio, and they were saying armed, and they were saying dangerous, and they were saying a reward.

She sat down on the mat.

"He said nothing," Mansa said to the empty room. "He always said nothing. Maybe that was the whole thing."

Monday had been hot.

35

She had not slept. That was where it started. Kwame had gone out at twenty to twelve — not slamming the door, which was worse, closing it the careful way he closed everything — and she had sat on the porch with her hair half done and the pot going cold on the stove, and then she had got up, because sitting still was not possible that night.

She walked. Not far. Past the compound, along the cemetery road, as far as the uncompleted houses — the ones that had been going up for four years and had never got past the first floor, the ones everybody said were bad luck.

There were torches behind them.

She stood still in the dark and watched men unloading a truck. Cement. Coils of wire. A generator, two of them straining at it. Working quietly and fast, the way men work when they do not want to be seen.

And she knew one of them.

Not well. Well enough. He had carried a bag of cement for her at the market once and had not wanted paying for it. She would have known that walk anywhere.

In the room she stood for a long time in the dark with her heart going, and then she dressed, and then she did her hair properly, and then she put on perfume.

People would say afterwards that it meant something. It did not mean anything. She put on perfume because she was going out, and because she was going to meet a man, and because she was thirty-eight years old and she was not going to meet a man at midnight looking as though she had been sitting up all night.

And while Kwame was still at the rank, before he came home, she had taken the little tin of oil they kept for the hinges and oiled the compound gate. Because the gate screamed. Because she did not want the whole compound to know she was going out at midnight to meet a man about a thing she had not told her husband.

Shame makes you careful about noise. That was all it was.

Then she told the wrong person.

His name was not a name she had any reason to distrust. He was a man from the compound who had once told her — years ago, when her purse was taken at Agbogbloshie — that if ever she needed anything sorted, she should call him, any hour, and he would sort it.

He answered on the third ring.

She told him what she had seen behind the uncompleted houses. She told him whose face she had recognised in the torchlight. She said she would not tell anybody.

She said thank you.

Then she set Kwame's phone back on the bedside table — and it was warm from her hand, and she did not think about that either — and she went out through the gate she had oiled, and it made no sound at all.

The man who came out of the dark at the end of the lane was not the man she was expecting.

He said her name. He put a hand on her arm.

It rang again, in his pocket.

He looked at it.

She said it.

Because he had not come back.

He took the phone away. The door shut. The bolt went across on the outside.

Mansa sat on the mat with her hands in her lap.

Out in Mallam Town a hundred thousand people were hearing her say that she no longer knew the man she had married, and every one of them was believing it, and the whole town would stop looking for Mansa Asante, because Mansa Asante had said so herself, in her own voice, on the air.

"Kwame," she said.

That night Kwabena Dapaah planed a piece of wood he did not need to plane.

Again. Again. Again. His hands kept going long after the wood was smooth, and the shavings came off in long pale curls and lay on the floor around his feet.

His wife stood in the doorway of the workshop and watched him.

"You have not slept properly in three nights."

"I am fine."

She did not believe him. Neither did he, particularly.

54

She left it there. He planed the same piece of wood until midnight, until his hands ached, until there was nothing left on it to take off.

The second night, the same bench. The same restlessness. The wood was already thinner than it should have been.

The third night he put the plane down and sat with his hands flat on the bench, staring at nothing, breathing like a man about to lift something too heavy for one person.

On the fourth morning he picked up his basket and walked back to Nene's compound.

Kwame rose when he came in, the way a man rises when he already knows what is coming and wants to meet it standing.

Kwabena stood just inside the doorway with the basket in his hand and did not open it.

"I came for my hands," he said.

A beat. Both men knew that was not why he had come.

Kwabena forced the words out flat and hard, the way you pull a nail out of old wood.

"I built the door."

Nene, at the back of the room, stopped what she was doing.

Kwame said nothing at all.

"Not your room," Kwabena said. "Not anybody's room. The third house behind the cemetery. The one with the wall that does not match."

He looked at his hands.

55

"Sarpong came to me four years ago. He said he wanted a way into that house that nobody would find. A way in for storing things, he said. Building materials. He said the site was being robbed blind and he wanted a place only he could get to."

He opened his hands and closed them again.

"I did not ask. That is the thing I have been living with. I did not ask, because a man pays you and you do not ask him questions. And I had three children in school that year."

"And when did you ask?" Nene said, from the back of the room.

Kwabena's mouth moved.

"When the boy went. The first one." He looked at her. "Everybody in Mallam Town heard about the boy. And I had built a door in a wall, and I knew then what the door was for, and I had been paid half of what he promised, and the other half had never come, and by then —"

He stopped.

"By then you had been paid," Nene said.

Kwabena Dapaah nodded.

Kwame said, very quietly: "Where is it?"

Kwabena told him.

"Behind the third house. At the back. There is a door in the wall, and it is flush, and the wood is matched so carefully you could stand on it and not see the seam. You would never find it unless you knew to look."

He lifted the basket.

"They keep things in there."

Chapter Twelve

The Narrow Escape

Kwame wanted to go that night.

"The door is in the wall," he said. "We know where it is. Every hour we wait is an hour they can move whatever is in there."

Nene looked at him for a while.

"I am not climbing through a hole in a fence at my age," she said. "You go. I will be here when you come back."

"And if somebody comes?"

"Then I will say I saw nothing." She went back to the mortar. "And they will believe me, because who tells an old woman anything?"

The third house was the one with the wall that did not match.

57

Kwame found it at dusk by walking along the back of the row with his hand flat on the plaster, the way Kwabena had told him. He passed it twice before he felt it — a seam, or less than a seam, a place where his fingernail caught.

He pressed.

It gave.

The room inside was dark and smelled of cement dust and old rainwater. He stood still for a moment letting his eyes adjust, and then he got his phone light out and swept it across the floor.

Bags of cement, stacked four high. Coils of wire. A generator under a sheet. Building materials for houses that are never going to be finished, made out of things that had been stolen from houses that were.

And in the far corner, under the window, a heap of car parts.

He crouched down beside it and put out one hand.

A door panel. A bumper. A seat, ripped out at the bolts. A wheel trim. And a side mirror, cracked across the glass.

He picked the mirror up.

It was his.

He had polished that mirror on a Monday morning with a rag far cleaner than the car deserved, sitting on an overturned crate at the rank, listening to a preacher he did not entirely believe — a Monday morning out of another life, three weeks gone and more. He knew the chip in the plastic housing at the corner — he had put his thumb over that chip a thousand times.

He stood up with the mirror in his hand.

58

Then his light caught something else, folded and pushed into the corner behind the seat.

He knew that cloth before he touched it.

It was her wrapper. The blue one with the Sunday pattern. It was dusty, and it had been folded — not thrown, folded — and he picked it up in both hands and put his face into it.

And there was nothing.

That was the thing. There was nothing.

Her perfume had been so strong in that room the first night you could almost taste it. Then it had faded. And now it was gone from the cloth too, and the cloth smelled only of cement dust.

She had been here.

She was not here now.

He heard the car before he saw it.

Not an engine — a tyre on gravel, the particular scrape of something heavy moving slowly. He killed the phone light and stood perfectly still in the dark with her wrapper in his hand.

It came up the track with no headlights.

Slow. Unhurried. Confident.

The way they had come up behind him on Dangerous Lane.

Kwame went out through the back of the third house, through a gap in the wall he had dropped a passenger at three years ago, and he ran.

Through the alley between the compounds where the washing lines hang low enough to catch you in the face. Past the food stall on the corner, where the woman looked up with her hand still in the pot and saw him, and looked back down into the pot again very quickly.

59

The Mallam Town reflex. See nothing. Survive.

Behind him: car doors. A torch beam. Voices, low and urgent. Not shouting. Professionals do not shout.

He went left, then left again, and came out at the zinc fence with the hole in it, and got down and went through on his hands and knees, and the fence caught his shirt and tore it, and he was up and running again with the wrapper still in his hand —

— and there were two of them at the end of the alley, coming the other way.

He stopped.

They did not hurry. That was the worst of it. They simply closed the gap, one from the front and one from behind, the way you close a door.

Kwame stood with his back to the fence.

Then, from somewhere behind the men, he heard a voice.

It was not raised. It was an old woman's voice, and it was not raised, and it said:

"Good evening."

The men turned.

Nene was standing at the mouth of the alley with her stick under one arm.

And behind her, filling the alley, the whole compound.

60

Maame Adjoa and Maame Akua, side by side. Ama from the MTN kiosk with her bad back. The woman from the food stall with the pot still in her hand. Two old men. A boy on a bicycle. Somebody's daughter with a baby on her hip. Ten people, then twenty, and more coming, and every one of them standing in the open with their faces showing. Somebody held up a phone light, and then somebody else did, and the alley filled with small white lights.

Nene had gone door to door.

"I am looking for my daughter," Nene said. She did not raise her voice. "She came this way. Has anybody seen her?"

Nobody said a word.

The two men looked at the alley, and at the faces, and at Nene. Then they simply went. Not running — walking, quickly, the way men walk away from a thing they had not expected. The crowd opened and closed behind them like water.

And then it was quiet.

Kwame slid down the fence and sat on the ground.

Nene came forward, leaning on her stick, and stood over him.

"You said you would sit," he said.

"I said I would be here when you came back." She looked down at him. "You thought I would sit."

They walked home with the whole compound around them, the way you walk a child home from something.

At Nene's gate the crowd broke up slowly and reluctantly, the way crowds do when something has happened and nobody wants to be the first to leave.

61

Kwame sat down on the low wall with Mansa's wrapper in his hands.

Nene went inside and came back with two cups.

"She was there," Kwame said.

"I know."

"Yesterday. Today. I do not know which. She was there." He put his hand flat on the cloth. "They folded it, Nene. Somebody folded it and put it in the corner."

Nene said nothing.

"And the car. My car is in there. The mirror is in there." He looked at her. "I held my own mirror in my hand."

Outside, the compound was going quiet. Somewhere a radio was being turned down for the night.

"Tomorrow," Nene said, "we take it to the police station. All of it. With all of them behind you."

Kwame nodded.

Then there was a knock at the door.

Not the way neighbours knock. Not the way the men knocked.

Three taps. A pause. A voice.

"Police."

Chapter Thirteen

The Honest Inspector

The knock came again.

Kwame was on his feet and halfway to the back of the room before Nene had even put her cup down.

"Sit down," she said.

"That is the police."

"I know what it is." She went to the door and opened it. "Sit down."

Outside in the dark there was a woman in uniform.

She was young — thirty, perhaps thirty-two — and she stood with her hands at her sides and her cap under one arm, and she had not come in.

"Good evening, ma," she said. "I am looking for Kwame Asante."

Nene did not move.

"Inspector Adzo Mensah," the woman said. "Mallam Town Police Post."

Behind Nene, Kwame stopped breathing.

63

Inspector Mensah looked past her into the room and saw him standing in the half-dark with a blue wrapper in his hands.

"Mr Asante," she said. "I am not here to arrest anyone. May I come in?"

Nene stood aside.

She sat on the low stool, because it was the only thing to sit on, and put her cap on her knee.

"I have been reading the file on Efua Nanfuri for three weeks," she said. "Every page. Nobody asked me to. That is not a virtue, it is just how I am, and it is why I am here."

She opened a folder on her knee.

"Mr Asante. You reported your taxi stolen on Thursday morning. Efua Nanfuri died on Monday night — the Monday after your car was taken, not the Monday of it. Four days after you stood in that station."

"Yes."

"Four days." She looked up. "You reported that taxi stolen four days before the robbery it was used in. A man who means to use his own car in a robbery does not put his own name against it in a police ledger four days early."

Kwame said nothing.

"Then there is this."

She turned a page.

"A clinic record. A nurse attended a head injury at this address on the Wednesday morning. Concussion observations. Two bruised ribs. A dislocated shoulder, set and bound. Documented on the Wednesday."

She looked at him.

64

"Efua Nanfuri died on Monday night. You could not have been in a car in Accra on Monday night with a shoulder that had been out of its socket since the Tuesday before."

Kwame turned and stared at Nene.

Nene was sorting leaves.

"I do not pretend about heads," she said, without looking up.

"So," Nene said. "You knew."

"I suspected," Inspector Mensah said. "Suspicion is not proof. And my Chief Inspector does not hear suspicion. He has a daughter in the ground."

She closed the folder.

"What I do not have is the rest of it. Who took the car. Why. Where the girl was going that night. And —" she looked at Kwame — "where your wife is. Because the whole town believes she walked out on you, and I have never believed that either."

Nene set the leaves down.

"Kwesi and Ekow," she said.

Inspector Mensah's head came up.

"Seventeen and nineteen. Apprentices at the shop by the rank — the one in the blue container. A year ago last March they stopped coming home. Before that they were working nights at the uncompleted houses behind the cemetery. Carrying things. For cash. For a man who came in a car and never got out of it."

"Who?"

"They were told it was the landlord." Nene looked at her. "Yaw Sarpong."

Inspector Mensah did not write it down. She went very still — the way Nene had gone still in the alley.

65

"Six months ago," Nene said, "a construction worker. The same place. And there is a door in a wall at the back of the third house, that a carpenter built four years ago and has been sorry about every day since."

She nodded at the table.

Kwame put the side mirror down. Then the wrapper.

Inspector Mensah looked at them and did not touch them.

"That is my mirror," Kwame said. "I found it tonight in the third house with the rest of my car. I polished that mirror myself, three weeks and more ago, with a rag far cleaner than the car deserved. And that is my wife's cloth, and somebody folded it before they left it in a corner."

She sat for a long moment.

Then she opened the folder again and took out a single sheet.

"This afternoon I ran the number from your phone through the official register. It took two hours and I was not supposed to do it." Her mouth was flat. "The number belongs to one Nartey, of this compound."

"Two doors from us," Kwame said.

"He is known to us." She looked at Nene, then back at Kwame. "He has been paid by Yaw Sarpong for four years. Rent collection. Debt. Carrying messages."

Nene picked the leaves up again.

"You have the paper," she said. "I have the people. Neither of us had enough alone. Together, I think it is enough."

Inspector Mensah stood up.

66

"My Chief Inspector will not hear this from me," she said. "He has put your face on every station in Accra. If I walk into his office tomorrow and tell him he was wrong, he will not take it off again — and he will take me off the case, and then there will be nobody at all."

"So what do we do?" Kwame said.

"We do not go to him." She put her cap on. "We bring him. In front of witnesses. In daylight. Where he cannot look away, and where there are too many people for anybody to say afterwards that it did not happen."

Kwame stood up.

"If saying this out loud costs me something," he said, "then let it cost me. I am tired of being quiet."

Inspector Mensah looked at him for a moment. Then she nodded once.

"Dawn," she said. "Be there at dawn, all of you. I will bring him."

When she had gone, Nene stood in the doorway for a long time, looking out at the dark with her hands folded on the top of her stick.

"Dawn," she said.

Then she went inside and picked the stick up properly.

"Everything in this town happens in the dark," she said. "Let us have this one in the light, for once."

Chapter Fourteen

Dawn at the Uncompleted House

They went out at first light.

Kwame had expected a dozen people. There were a hundred before they reached the main road, and more coming out of the compounds as they passed, and by the cemetery wall it was not a crowd any more, it was a town.

Nene led it, leaning on her stick, going slower than anybody.

68

Behind her came Maame Adjoa and Maame Akua with their arms linked. Ama from the MTN kiosk. The woman from the food stall with her pot. Kwabena Dapaah with his tools in a basket, walking with his head down. Papa Kofi and Mr. Tee from the rank, shoulder to shoulder, not arguing for once. The Old Woman on the veranda, who had not walked further than her own gate in two years and was walking this morning. Children who should have been getting ready for school.

Nobody had told them to come. Word had gone round Mallam Town the way word goes round, and Mallam Town had decided to see.

Chief Inspector Nanfuri's car was already there.

He got out slowly. He looked older than he had looked in his office, and he stood for a moment taking in a hundred people with the flat disbelief of a man who had asked for order and been given a town.

Then he saw Kwame.

"This is a crime scene," Nanfuri said. "I am not —"

"Chief Inspector."

Kwame stepped forward out of the crowd.

He was unarmed. He held his hands out from his sides with the palms turned up, the way a man does when there is nothing in them.

"You put my face on the radio," Kwame said, "and you called me a murderer."

Nanfuri's jaw set.

"I am here to show you whose hands did it."

Nobody spoke.

69

Nanfuri looked at Kwame, and at the hundred people, and at Inspector Adzo Mensah, who stood beside her Chief Inspector with her cap under her arm and said nothing at all.

Then Kwabena Dapaah stepped forward with his basket.

He went to the back wall of the third house. He put the basket down. He took out a chisel, fitted it into the seam, and pressed.

The door opened.

Kwabena stood back.

"I built it," he said. "Four years ago. He paid me half."

He did not look at anybody while he said it.

Nanfuri went to the doorway and looked in, and stood there for a long time.

Cement, stacked four high. Coils of wire. A generator under a sheet. And a heap of car parts in the corner, and among them a yellow door panel with a dent in it, and a side mirror cracked across the glass.

Inspector Adzo Mensah said, without being asked:

"The dent is on the rear passenger door, sir. That is what Mr Asante described to the Desk Officer on the Thursday morning. It is in the ledger."

Nanfuri did not move.

"Sir," Mensah said. "There is somebody else in here."

There was an inner room, windowless, with a door that locked on the outside. They got it open.

She was sitting on a mat against the far wall with her hands folded in her lap. When the light came in she put up one hand to shield her face. Then she saw who was standing in the doorway.

70

The crowd made a sound. Not a cheer — something else. The sound a hundred people make when they have all been wrong about the same thing at the same moment.

Kwame went in and knelt down in front of her and did not touch her.

"Mansa," he said.

"I did not go." Her voice was not working properly. "I did not go. They made me say it on the radio. Kwame, I did not go —"

"I know."

"I thought you left."

"I came back."

They looked at each other across four feet of concrete floor with a hundred people watching, and neither of them moved, because there was too much to move through first.

Then Maame Adjoa said, from somewhere behind him, in a voice that was not loud:

"What is that?"

They all turned.

In the corner of the inner room, beside the mat, there was a mechanic's toolbag. Canvas, gone soft with use. And on the side of it, painted in letters that had faded but not gone:

KWESI

The crowd went quiet.

Maame Adjoa went past Kwame as though he were not there and picked the bag up in both hands and held it against herself. Then she sat down on the concrete with it and put her face into it, and Maame Akua knelt beside her with one hand on her back, and neither of them made any sound at all.

Nene stood in the doorway with her stick and watched them.

"I have been angry about that for a long time," she said quietly.

71

She looked at the bag with the boy's name on it.

"Now it has a name on it."

They brought Mansa out into the daylight.

Somebody gave her a coat. She sat on an upturned bucket with the coat round her shoulders and the whole of Mallam Town in front of her, and Inspector Adzo Mensah took out a notebook, and Mansa Asante told the truth in her own voice, in front of everybody.

She told them she had not slept. That she had walked as far as the uncompleted houses and had seen men unloading a truck in the dark with torches, and had known one of the faces.

She told them she had gone home, and dressed, and that she had put on perfume because she was going out to meet a man, and not for any other reason in the world.

She told them that while Kwame was still at the rank she had oiled the compound gate, because it screamed, and because she did not want the compound to hear her go, and because she was ashamed of going behind her husband's back — and shame makes you careful about noise.

"I opened it myself," she said. "That is why it did not scream. He did not leave me. I went."

She told them she had used Kwame's phone because her credit had finished, and that she had called Nartey, two doors away, because he had told her years ago that if she ever needed anything sorted she should call him, any hour.

72

"I told the wrong person," Mansa said. "That is all I did wrong. I told the wrong person, and I did not tell my husband."

Then the last thing.

"And the calls." She looked at Kwame. "The two times he rang." Her chin came up. "I did not press anything. I could not reach the phone. The man who took me pressed it, both times, and put it in his own pocket."

Kwame closed his eyes.

Chief Inspector Nanfuri had not moved since the door opened.

He stood with his hands at his sides and looked at the yellow door panel, and at the woman on the bucket, and at the old woman on the concrete with a boy's toolbag in her arms, and at a hundred people from a town he was supposed to be policing.

Then he took out his radio.

"Chief Inspector —" somebody began.

He held up one hand.

He spoke into it. He gave his name and his rank. He said that a stolen vehicle had been recovered, that Kwame Asante was cleared of all charges with immediate effect, and that an arrest was to be made at the compound of Yaw Sarpong.

Then he put the radio away and turned to Kwame.

"I put your photograph on the radio and I called you a murderer," he said. "I did it because the simplest story was the easiest one to grieve with. That is not a reason."

He did not ask to be forgiven.

"I will say it myself, on every station that carried your name. Every one."

73

Kwame nodded.

"I am sorry about your daughter," he said.

Nanfuri's mouth did something. He looked away, then looked back, and held out his hand, and Kwame took it, and it was brief and it was firm, and that was all of it.

Then somebody in the crowd — Papa Kofi, of course — shouted:

"Peacemaker!"

And the crowd took it up. Not laughing. Not mocking. The way a town says a thing it has always said.

Peacemaker. Peacemaker.

Kwame stood with his hands still open at his sides.

And he heard it the way he had never heard it before. Twenty years of a nickname meaning: the man who keeps quiet. The man who swallows it. The man who settles other people's fights while losing his own by default.

He looked at Mansa on the bucket. At Nene in the doorway. At the two mothers on the concrete with a boy's toolbag between them.

"No," Kwame said.

The crowd quietened.

"I spent my whole life thinking peace meant keeping quiet." He said it plainly, and his voice carried the way it always had — the way it carried at the rank when two men had run out of words. "I do not believe that anymore."

Chapter Fifteen

The Okada

It happened while the crowd was still there.

Kwame heard it before he saw it — the whine of a small engine coming up the track too fast, the particular sound an okada makes when the rider is not thinking about the road.

It came round the end of the third house and stopped in a spray of gravel.

Yaw Sarpong got off the back of it.

75

He was fifty-six and well fed, and he was wearing the face of a man arriving to deal with a small problem. Then he saw the door standing open in the wall. He saw the cement and the wire and the generator under its sheet. He saw the yellow door panel with the dent in the rear passenger door, laid out on the ground where Inspector Adzo Mensah had put it.

And he saw Mansa Asante sitting on the upturned bucket in the daylight with somebody's coat around her shoulders.

He turned and ran.

The crowd did not close.

That was the thing Kwame remembered afterwards, and the thing he went on remembering for years — that not one person in a hundred put out a hand. No shout. No stone. Nothing at all.

They simply parted, the way a crowd parts, and let him through. Because there was nowhere left for him to go, and everybody standing there knew it.

He got back on the bike.

It fishtailed at once on the loose gravel of the track — the track he had never had surfaced in four years, because a surfaced track is a track people remember — and went down hard on its side, and Sarpong went down with it, and the bike went on without him in a long skid of sparks and dust.

The car coming up behind him was not going fast.

That did not matter.

76

The sound was not a scream. It was a noise Kwame had heard once, years ago, at the rank, and had never managed to forget: the ordinary, muffled sound of a body in the way of something heavy.

Then dust, and quiet, and a hundred people standing absolutely still.

Nene was the first to move.

She went forward leaning on her stick, and she knelt — which took her a while, and hurt, and she said so to nobody — and she put two fingers against the side of Sarpong's neck.

Exactly as she had done for Kwame in the gutter.

Somebody behind her said it, breathless and half-pleased:

"It is finished for him."

Nene did not look up.

"It is not finished for him," she said. "It is beginning."

She shifted her weight, and Kwame saw what it cost her to stay down there, and she did not get up.

"He is still a man. Somebody call the hospital."

They said afterwards that he would not walk again.

Kwame never heard anybody say they were sorry about it. He never heard anybody say they were glad.

The ambulance came forty minutes late, because this was Mallam Town.

Inspector Adzo Mensah took Sarpong's statement where he lay on the track, with her notebook on her knee and the crowd standing well back, because that was her job and she did it properly. She took Nartey's name a second time. She wrote down every word of Kwabena Dapaah's account, and made him sign it.

77

Then there was nothing left to do there, and the sun was properly up, and a hundred people began the walk back into Mallam Town.

At the main road Nene stopped and sat down on the low wall, and everybody waited, because by then everybody waited for Nene.

"My knees," she said, to nobody in particular. "I have been telling you people about my knees for a year and nobody listens to me."

A child ran past and she told him to slow down, and he slowed down.

A woman came up from the market with three yams in a cloth and pressed them on her, and Nene said it was too much, and the woman said it was not nearly enough, and they went back and forth about it for a while.

Kwame stood in the road with Mansa's wrapper folded over his arm and watched her.

That is the whole point of her, he thought.

Mansa was walking a little way ahead with Maame Akua on one side and Maame Adjoa on the other, and the three of them were not talking about anything that had happened. Kwame watched them and did not catch up. There would be time for that. There would be a long time for it, and it would not be easy, and it was beginning — which was the thing that mattered.

They came to the rank. The drivers were out and the horns were going and the kenkey seller was calling her prices, and Mallam Town was being Mallam Town as though nothing at all had happened.

78

At the end of the rank, Kwame stopped.

The gate was still there. Rusted, crooked at the top, the post bent beyond repair — the same gate he had pushed open slowly every night of his adult life, muffling the sound with his own hand so as not to wake the compound.

He put his hand flat on it.

Then he pushed, and it screamed — a long metal shriek that went the whole length of the rank and out into the road, loud and rusty and impossible to ignore.

Two men at the far end looked up. Papa Kofi said something to Mr. Tee. Somewhere a dog started up.

This time, everybody heard.

79

Glossary

Part A — words from Ghana. Part B — difficult words. Part C — the names. Part D — Nene’s medicine. Words are explained the way this book uses them, not the way a dictionary would.

Part A — Words from Ghana

apprentice — a young person learning a trade by working under somebody who is already skilled, usually for little or no pay. Kwesi and Ekow are apprentices at a mechanic's shop.

Chief Inspector — a senior officer in the Ghana Police Service. Above an Inspector, below an Assistant Superintendent.

compound / compound house — a house built around an open yard, with the rooms all opening onto that yard. Several families usually live in one compound and share the yard, the kitchen and the bathhouse. The yard is the place where everybody sees everybody.

Desk Officer — the police officer at the front desk of a station, who takes reports from the public. In this book, the Desk Officer writes in a ledger with a blue Biro that skips.

gutter — the open drain at the side of a road. In this book the gutter is where Mallam Town puts things it does not want to look at.

highlife — a popular Ghanaian music style that mixes guitar bands, horns and Akan rhythms. It has been the sound of Ghana's bars and taxis for nearly a hundred years.

Inspector — a police officer ranking below a Chief Inspector.

kenkey — a Ghanaian food made from fermented maize dough, wrapped in corn husks or plantain leaves and boiled. It is usually eaten with fried fish and pepper sauce. The kenkey seller in this book walks the rank calling out her prices.

kiosk — a small stall or booth at the side of the road. An MTN kiosk sells mobile phone credit, SIM cards and Mobile Money services.

Mallam Town — a real township in the Greater Accra Region, on the road out of Accra. In this book it is the place where Kwame and Mansa live.

MoMo — short for Mobile Money: sending and receiving money on a mobile phone. Very common in Ghana. People pay for almost anything with it, and people ask each other about their MoMo balance.

mortar and pestle — a heavy bowl (the mortar) and a short club (the pestle), used for pounding things. Nene pounds bark into a paste in hers. The mortar in her room is worn smooth on one side from years of use.

MTN — one of Ghana's largest mobile phone networks.

80

okada — a motorcycle that carries passengers for money, the way a taxi does. Motorcycle taxis are called okada across West Africa. They are fast, they are cheap, and they are dangerous.

Papa — a respectful name for an older man, whether or not he is really your father. That is why a driver at the rank is called Papa Kofi.

police post — a small local police station, smaller than a district station.

rank — the place where taxis and trotro gather to wait for passengers. Twenty years at the rank is what taught Kwame how to settle an argument.

trotro — a shared minibus that runs a fixed route and picks passengers up along the way. The name is said to come from the old fare of threepence.

uncompleted house — a building somebody started and never finished. In many Ghanaian towns you can see them standing for years with no roof, no windows and no one living in them. Behind the cemetery in this book there are four of them.

veranda — a covered porch or passage along the front of a house, often with a low wall you can sit on. The Old Woman in this book sits on her veranda and watches everything that goes past.

wrapper — a large piece of cloth that a woman wraps around herself as a skirt, or over her shoulders. Also simply called "cloth." In this book, Mansa's blue wrapper is the only thing Kwame finds of hers.

yam — a starchy root vegetable, like a very large sweet potato, boiled or pounded into fufu. In this book Nene is paid in yam, and complains that it is not nearly enough.

zinc — corrugated metal sheeting, used for roofs and fences. It is called zinc in Ghana even though it is really galvanised steel.

81

Part B — Difficult words in this book

abandoned — left somewhere and never come back for.

absolutely — completely; totally; with no exception.

accusation — a statement saying that somebody did something wrong.

arithmetic — working with numbers. In this book it is used to mean working out the safest thing to do.

ashamed — feeling bad because you have done something you think is wrong.

bulletin — a short news report on the radio or television.

complicated — having many parts; hard to understand or deal with.

concussion — an injury to the head that makes a person confused, dizzy or sleepy. It can be serious. Nene watches Kwame's pupils through the night because she is checking for it.

contradict — to say the opposite of what somebody else has said.

deliberate — careful and unhurried; done on purpose, not by accident.

disbelief — the feeling of not being able to believe what you are seeing.

dislocated — pulled out of its joint. A dislocated shoulder is a shoulder that has come out of its socket. Nene puts Kwame's back in.

documented — written down officially, so that it can be used as proof.

fishtailed — slid sideways, with the back end swinging out. A motorcycle fishtails when it loses grip.

immediate — happening at once, with no delay.

irritable — easily annoyed; bad-tempered.

muttered — said something quietly and not clearly, usually because you are annoyed.

newsreader — the person who reads the news on the radio or television.

official — done or approved by somebody in authority. An official record is one the police or a hospital will accept.

overturned — tipped over; knocked onto its side.

potholes — holes in the surface of a road.

pretended — acted as if something were true when it was not.

professional — doing a job for money, and doing it properly. In this book the men who come for Kwame are professionals, and "professionals do not shout."

pulse — the beat of blood in your body, which you can feel at your wrist or at the side of your neck. Checking somebody's pulse is how you tell whether they are still alive. Nene checks Kwame's in the gutter: "she put two fingers against the side of his neck and held them there, counting to herself." Fourteen chapters later she does exactly the same thing for the man who ordered it — "Exactly as she had done for Kwame in the gutter."

82

reluctantly — unwillingly; doing something you do not really want to do.

restlessness — the feeling of not being able to keep still or settle.

separated — pulled apart; made to be apart.

simmered — cooked gently, just below boiling.

suspicion — a feeling that something is true, without being able to prove it.

unarmed — carrying no weapon.

unhurried — not rushed; calm and slow.

upturned — turned over, so the bottom faces up.

vibrating — shaking, from nervousness or from holding something in too long.

windowless — having no windows.

witnesses — people who saw something happen, and can say so.

Part D — Nene's medicine
